title: Praying the Psalms (Psalm 23)
hookLine: for three thousand years people have prayed with borrowed words

lines: THE PRAYER BOOK INSIDE THE BIBLE.
cards: Think of the times you had no words of your own. At a funeral. In the night after bad news.
On a day so good you wanted to shout. People often reach for borrowed words: a song, a poem, someone else's line that says it better.
At funerals in many countries, even people who never go to church find they know one set of words by heart. The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
Those words come from a book of a hundred and fifty prayers and songs, prayed in one form or another for close to three thousand years: the prayer book inside the Bible.

teach.b: Psalter is the book of Psalms, used for praying. It comes from the Greek for a stringed instrument, because these were songs. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises.
Tradition links many to King David, the shepherd boy who became king around three thousand years ago, though many were written by others, over centuries.
Surprise: they're not all praise. There's joy, but also rage, fear, loneliness, and complaints that sound almost rude, words for every mood.
Jesus prayed them: his cry on the cross, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, is the first line of Psalm twenty-two. Jews have prayed the psalms every day for many centuries, and still do.
Monks under the Rule of Saint Benedict pray all hundred and fifty weekly; the Anglican prayer book walks through them every month.
Now the most well-known one, in the King James Bible: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters."
Where it prints LORD in capitals, the Hebrew has God's own personal name, which Jews, out of reverence, do not say aloud.

teach.h: IN THE VALLEY: THOU ART WITH ME.
teach.b: It doesn't pretend life is easy: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me." Notice the turn.
The first lines talk about God; in the dark valley, it talks to him: thou art with me.
That's what borrowed words can do. You start by reading. You end up talking.

how: Christians pray and sing the Psalms in worship every week, and monks and many others pray them daily; the Rule of Saint Benedict covers all 150 in a week, and the Book of Common Prayer in a month. Psalm 23 is read at many Christian funerals.

games.q: you're praying Psalm 23. it starts by talking about God: the Lord is my shepherd. then you reach the valley of the shadow of death. what does the psalm do?
o: it starts talking to God: thou art with me.
it asks to be rescued from the valley.
games.why: in the dark valley, the psalm turns from about God to toward God: I will fear no evil: for thou art with me.

practice: Find Psalm twenty-three, only six verses, and read it aloud at half speed, pausing at every comma, or just say the lines you heard today. Notice which phrase catches, and stay with it.
If you pray, let the psalm be your prayer; if not, a poem thousands have leaned on.
